title: Judges’ wages and debt law
summary: The law of Mosiah provides wages for judges according to time worked, sets out a procedure for unpaid debts, and specifies a judge’s daily wage.

The stated daily wage was a senine of gold or a senum of silver, which were equal in value.

title: Nephite reckoning
summary: The account names gold and silver units and explains their relative values, including their equivalence to grain measures.

explicit_facts.text: Nephites used a reckoning and measures distinct from those of the Jews at Jerusalem, altered according to the people’s minds and circumstances, and established by King Mosiah by the reign of the judges.
The listed gold units are the senine, seon, shum, and limnah; the listed silver units are the senum, amnor, ezrom, and onti.
A senum equaled a senine and either could purchase a measure of barley or any kind of grain.
A seon was twice a senine, a shum twice a seon, and a limnah equaled them all.
An amnor equaled two senums, an ezrom four senums, and an onti equaled them all.

reasonable_visual_inferences: A nonliteral explanatory graphic may compare the named units and grain measures.
unspecified_visual_details: The appearance, shape, and material of the monetary pieces; any containers or measuring vessels.

narration.text: A senum of silver, an amnor of silver, an ezrom of silver, and an onti of silver.

doctrinal_or_story_notes: These verses explain a system of reckoning; they do not describe a transaction occurring in the present scene.
prohibited_inventions: Do not show Jerusalem or King Mosiah as physically present; they are mentioned in the account, not shown in a narrated event.

title: Lesser units
summary: The account lists lesser units of value, including their relationships to one another and to a measure of barley.

explicit_facts.text: A shiblon was half a senum and corresponded to half a measure of barley; a shiblum was half a shiblon; a leah was half a shiblum.
An antion of gold equaled three shiblons.
